title: How Discoveries Are Made: The Passive Voice in Science
paragraphs: In 1928, a petri dish was left near an open window in a London laboratory. Penicillin was not invented — it was discovered. A mould had grown on the dish, and bacteria around the mould had been killed. Alexander Fleming noticed what had happened. From this accidental observation, a drug was developed that would go on to save hundreds of millions of lives. The passive voice dominates this story for a reason: the discovery was made by circumstances as much as by any individual, and the passive allows the narrative to reflect this.

Scientific writing has used passive voice as its default register for well over a century, and the reasons are deeply embedded in the philosophy of scientific knowledge. Science claims to produce objective, reproducible findings — findings that are true regardless of who produced them. When a chemist writes "the solution was heated to 80°C," the identity of the chemist is irrelevant. What matters is that the solution was heated, to that temperature, in that way. The passive construction makes this epistemological claim visible in the grammar itself.

This does not mean all passive is appropriate in all scientific contexts. The style conventions of scientific writing have been shifting, particularly in recent decades. Many journals now actively encourage active voice in sections where the researcher's choices are the focus: "We designed the experiment to test three hypotheses." "We chose to include rural populations in the sample." Here, the first person active acknowledges that these were decisions — choices made by specific researchers — rather than procedures that simply happened.

A common complaint about passive voice in academic writing is that it is used to obscure accountability. "The data was misinterpreted." "The results were inadequately reported." "The conflict of interest was not disclosed." Each of these passives hides the agent who made the error. Critics argue that this kind of passive is a mechanism of institutional self-protection — a way of acknowledging that something went wrong while avoiding the assignment of individual responsibility.

The passive is also central to how scientific consensus is communicated: "It has been established that smoking causes cancer." "It has been demonstrated that sleep deprivation impairs cognitive function." "It is now widely accepted that climate change is human-caused." These impersonal passive constructions — it has been shown, it is believed, it has been confirmed — allow scientists to invoke the authority of a community of evidence rather than making a personal claim. The grammar performs the collective nature of scientific knowledge.

For students at B1 level, the practical implication is this: learn to read passive constructions not just grammatically but epistemically. When you read "it has been suggested that X," ask: by whom? With what evidence? With what degree of certainty? The passive construction is not merely a choice of form — it is a choice of how to present knowledge, and knowledge presented differently carries different authority, different certainty, and different political implications.

The discovery of penicillin was not a single moment. It was a process — involving Fleming's observation, subsequent laboratory work by others, clinical trials, manufacturing innovations, and distribution decisions. Each of these stages can be narrated in passive: "the compound was isolated, was tested, was approved, was manufactured, was distributed." The passive traces the journey of an object — the drug — through the processes that made it what it eventually became.

dialogue.speaker: Zhibek
dialogue.text: I read that scientific journals are now encouraging active voice. But my ecology supervisor wants passive. Who's right?

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: Both, in different sections. For methods: passive — "samples were collected, data was processed." For interpretation: active — "we argue that X."

dialogue.speaker: Zhibek
dialogue.text: So passive for the procedure, active for the argument?

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: Exactly. Passive says: here's what happened, objectively. Active says: here's what we think it means.

dialogue.speaker: Zhibek
dialogue.text: What about when passive hides errors — like "the data was misinterpreted"?

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: That's the political use. The passive removes the agent and diffuses accountability. Which is why it gets criticised.

dialogue.speaker: Zhibek
dialogue.text: So knowing passive well means knowing when NOT to use it too.

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: Yes. Passive is a precision tool. Using it without thinking is just as bad as avoiding it entirely.

keyPhrases.context: "Epistemological claim." = a claim about the nature and source of knowledge.
"Reproducible findings." = results that can be replicated by other scientists.
"Default register of scientific writing." = the typical style or level of language used.
"Used to obscure accountability." = to make something less clear or hide it.
"Scientific consensus." = general agreement among scientists based on evidence.
"Invokes the authority of evidence." = calls upon or refers to for support.
"Read not just grammatically but epistemically." = thinking about the nature of the knowledge.
"Avoid the assignment of individual accountability." = being responsible and answerable.

vocab.definition: able to be repeated with the same results
vocab.example: "Reproducible findings" — results that hold true regardless of who runs the experiment.

vocab.definition: to make difficult to see or understand; to hide
vocab.example: "Passive is used to obscure accountability." — it hides who made the error.

vocab.definition: being responsible and required to explain your actions
vocab.example: "A way of avoiding individual accountability." — passive hides who is responsible.
"Scientific consensus." — what the scientific community broadly agrees on.

vocab.definition: a substance formed from two or more elements chemically united
vocab.example: "The compound was isolated, tested, approved, manufactured." — penicillin's journey.

vocab.definition: the branch of philosophy concerned with the nature and extent of knowledge
vocab.example: "Epistemological claim." — about how we know what we know and what counts as knowledge.

vocab.definition: a fungus that grows on damp surfaces
vocab.example: "A mould had grown on the dish." — Fleming's famous penicillin discovery.

vocab.definition: to weaken or damage the ability to do something
vocab.example: "Sleep deprivation impairs cognitive function." — damages the ability to think.
